idiom_name: std::collections::HashMap entry API over cell tuples
implementation_notes: There is no spatial index in std or std::collections; the manual realization uses HashMap<(i32, i32), Vec<EntityId>> with the entry API for insert and cheap integer keys (doc.rust-lang.org HashMap). The borrow checker forces query code to collect ids before mutating entities, and for bounded worlds a Vec<Vec<EntityId>> grid avoids hashing entirely. The hand grid stays the default for frequently moving entities; the rstar variant provides a real R*-tree when queries are geometric.
pitfalls: Storing &mut Entity in cells fights the borrow checker; store EntityId (or an index) and resolve through a central arena instead.
HashMap uses SipHash by default; per-move hashing of small integer keys is measurable, so a Vec grid or a faster hasher pays off.
Stale ids after despawn surface as lookup failures deep in query code; remove from the grid in the same path that despawns.

variants.name: rstar R*-tree
variants.idiom_name: rstar::RTree with RTreeObject envelopes and locate_in_envelope
variants.implementation_notes: rstar's RTree is the de-facto Rust spatial index: stored objects implement RTreeObject with an AABB envelope, and the tree answers range queries via locate_in_envelope and nearest-neighbour searches (rstar docs). It replaces the hand grid for mostly static or geometry-shaped data; per-frame movers pay reinsertion and tree-rebalancing costs the hash grid does not have.
pitfalls: The envelope must be stable while the object is in the tree; mutating a position in place corrupts the index, so remove, mutate and reinsert.
remove requires an equal value (envelope plus identity fields), so keep the inserted representation retrievable.
locate_in_envelope returns objects whose envelopes intersect, which is a candidate set, not the exact result.
